Disaster Recovery Overview

or finances is a disaster

• 	RPO: Recovery Point Objective
• 	RTO: Recovery Time Objective

• 	Option 2:
• 	Create an Aurora MySQL DB

Transferring large amount of data into AWS
• 	Example: transfer 200 TB of data in the cloud. We have a 100 Mbps internet
connection.
• 	Over the internet / Site-to-Site VPN:
• 	Immediate to setup
• 	Will take 200(TB)*1000(GB)*1000(MB)*8(Mb)/100 Mbps = 16,000,000s = 185d
• 	Over direct connect 1Gbps:
• 	Long for the one-time setup (over a month)
• 	Will take 200(TB)*1000(GB)*8(Gb)/1 Gbps = 1,600,000s = 18.5d
• 	Over Snowball:
• 	Takes about 1 week for the end-to-end transfer
• 	Can be combined with DMS
• 	For on-going replication / transfers: Site-to-Site VPN or DX with DMS or
DataSync

content.summary:
## Recovery objectives and strategy cost

RPO bounds acceptable data loss; RTO bounds acceptable recovery time. Tighter objectives generally require more ongoing replication, ready capacity and operational coordination, which must be tested rather than assumed.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

The relaxed objectives can justify a lower standby cost, provided restoration meets the actual requirements. More expensive active-active operation may be unnecessary, while untested backups and missing dependencies cannot establish a recovery guarantee.

### Avoid this trap

Multi-AZ availability is not automatically a cross-Region disaster recovery plan. A replicated copy does not prove the runbook, dependency recovery and application validation meet the RTO.

### Apply it

A business accepts hours of recovery and a day of data loss for a low-priority system. Which approach is the reasonable low-cost starting point?

**Recommended design:** Evaluate tested backup-and-restore with retention and recovery procedures matching the objectives.

The relaxed objectives can justify a lower standby cost, provided restoration meets the actual requirements. More expensive active-active operation may be unnecessary, while untested backups and missing dependencies cannot establish a recovery guarantee.
keyPoints: RPO bounds acceptable data loss; RTO bounds acceptable recovery time. Tighter objectives generally require more ongoing replication, ready capacity and operational coordination, which must be tested rather than assumed.

The relaxed objectives can justify a lower standby cost, provided restoration meets the actual requirements. More expensive active-active operation may be unnecessary, while untested backups and missing dependencies cannot establish a recovery guarantee.
Multi-AZ availability is not automatically a cross-Region disaster recovery plan. A replicated copy does not prove the runbook, dependency recovery and application validation meet the RTO.

cards.question: How do RPO and RTO guide the choice among backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active?
cards.answer: RPO bounds acceptable data loss; RTO bounds acceptable recovery time. Tighter objectives generally require more ongoing replication, ready capacity and operational coordination, which must be tested rather than assumed. The relaxed objectives can justify a lower standby cost, provided restoration meets the actual requirements. More expensive active-active operation may be unnecessary, while untested backups and missing dependencies cannot establish a recovery guarantee.

cards.question: What failure mode or trade-off must you avoid when designing recovery objectives and strategy cost?
cards.answer: Multi-AZ availability is not automatically a cross-Region disaster recovery plan. A replicated copy does not prove the runbook, dependency recovery and application validation meet the RTO.

quiz.question: A business accepts hours of recovery and a day of data loss for a low-priority system. Which approach is the reasonable low-cost starting point?
options: Evaluate tested backup-and-restore with retention and recovery procedures matching the objectives.
Choose multi-Region active-active solely because every workload requires it.
Replicate data with no tested restore or application recovery process.
Treat an unmonitored local disk copy as a complete regional disaster plan.
quiz.explanation: The relaxed objectives can justify a lower standby cost, provided restoration meets the actual requirements. More expensive active-active operation may be unnecessary, while untested backups and missing dependencies cannot establish a recovery guarantee.

## Migration with change capture

Use an appropriate initial load plus change data capture when supported, validate ongoing replication and plan a controlled cutover. Assess schema conversion separately when source and target engines differ.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

Initial load plus CDC allows most transfer while the source stays active. Final synchronization and validation reduce cutover risk. Engine/schema differences require additional assessment, and a rollback decision is part of the migration plan.

### Avoid this trap

DMS is not a universal application or schema compatibility converter. Replication lag, unsupported objects, permissions and rollback must be evaluated before cutover.

### Apply it

A large database must migrate while production continues writing, with a short final cutover. Which approach should be evaluated?

**Recommended design:** Use a supported DMS full load plus CDC workflow, validate synchronization, then perform a planned cutover.

Initial load plus CDC allows most transfer while the source stays active. Final synchronization and validation reduce cutover risk. Engine/schema differences require additional assessment, and a rollback decision is part of the migration plan.
